articles.title: US discreetly moves diplomats and families from multiple Middle Eastern countries as intel warns of Iranian plots - CNN
articles.summary: US discreetly moves diplomats and families from multiple Middle Eastern countries as intel warns of Iranian plots  CNNIran live updates: Iranian plotting against US citizens abroad in 'advanced stages'  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and VideosEXCLUSIVE: US orders diplomats to depart Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes  ReutersU.S. troops and diplomats evacuating Middle East posts, sources say  NBC NewsUS warns of Houthi threat in updated Israel travel...
articles.full_text:
The United States is rushing to move some diplomats and their family members from posts in the Middle East as the threat of regional escalation looms, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.
The departures have been described as a frustrating and chaotic déjà vu, as many of those leaving had only recently returned to their posts after being ordered out during the height of the Iran war.
An unclassified October 23 memo to Secretary of State Marco Rubio says US intelligence has found that “Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel” and plotting efforts “have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries.”
A US official told CNN, “When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment. The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO Status in the region.”
Axios was first to report on the unclassified memo.
“To say it has been chaotic is an understatement,” said one US diplomat, explaining that the financial support they have been offered to date does not cover the costs for moving their entire family from the region. Many of those families had scrambled then to leave their homes in the Middle East in the early weeks of the war and find new housing and schools for their kids. Now, many are having to do the same again, with what they say is potentially less financial support from the State Department.
“This echoes the chaos families experienced earlier this year. Some had barely settled back in before being told to leave again,” Nikki Gamer, the spokesperson for the American Foreign Service Association, told CNN. “They are understandably upset, confused, and angry.”
Later Friday, a State Department official confirmed that all US direct hire personnel and their families “are getting per diem allowances and support for lodging and schools, with per diem allowances consistent with government rates of where they are geographically in the country.”
The adjustments come as the Iranian-backed Houthis have increased their attacks on Saudi Arabia – hostilities which the State Department has repeatedly warned “have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area.”
They also come as US President Donald Trump has suggested he could relaunch strikes against Iran after the midterms, and as sources said Israel has lobbied – unsuccessfully for now – for more immediate action.
The State Department this week ordered the departure of non-emergency personnel and all family members from Saudi Arabia. Officials said the ordered departure was done in response to the Houthi escalations.
At the same time, it has been quietly adjusting its staffing caps at multiple other embassies in the Middle East, including Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, and Lebanon, sources told CNN.
A State Department official confirmed to CNN that Lebanon, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Jordan “will see temporary changes to staffing levels under restricted operations.” They said there are no changes to personnel in Kuwait or Bahrain, which suggest they are not over their staffing caps.
“Under Restricted Operations Status, staffing levels are constantly evaluated and adjusted,” the official said.
Unlike the Saudi Arabia ordered departure, the movements from these embassies have not been publicly announced. The State Department has stressed that those embassies, unlike Saudi Arabia, have not changed status and remain on “restricted operations” status. Even when there is no formal change in status, there can still be a change in staffing within the “restricted operations” status.
“There’s a very Groundhog Day vibe,” a source in Amman said of some embassy staff being asked to leave the Jordanian capital again.
Not all of the embassies allowed children to return to the posts, but most allowed spouses to come back. Now, the family members are leaving those embassies to which they have only recently been allowed to return – but unlike earlier this year, sources say family members are not being given the same financial support.
Communication and coordination around the departures from the department’s headquarters in Foggy Bottom to foreign service officers in the field is “just as much of a shit show” as early on in the Iran war, said one source familiar with the departures.
In the days around the adjustments, there were concerns among foreign service officers about whether the State Department will give their families “per diem” allowances for relocating to the US, the source said, noting that some embassies haven’t had the planning meetings or town halls with staff that are typical before departures.
“A lot of people are hearing about it through the news instead of their leadership at post,” the source added.
The American Foreign Service Association, the union representing foreign service officers, said it is hearing accounts “of bureaucratic ping-pong.”
“Families that had barely returned to their posts and re-enrolled their children in school are being told to prepare to evacuate again without being advised as to what level of financial support they can count on,” it said in a statement Thursday.
Gamer, the spokesperson for AFSA, told CNN that “families outside Saudi Arabia have told AFSA they are being directed to leave without confirmed housing assistance or per diem.” They have been told this is because their embassies are not changing status from “restricted operations.”
Families often rely on those allowances to help them find housing and cover the unexpected costs associated with being uprooted from their homes abroad, especially if their diplomatic family member is remaining at the embassy as an essential worker.
“Families deserve to know how they will pay for a place to live before they board a plane,” Gamer said.
The State Department official said, “We understand how hard being on Restricted Operations Status, Authorized Departure, or Ordered Departure is for our diplomatic staff and their families.”
“We are committed to using every tool available to help families navigate this difficult time, including the added expenses and school enrollment,” they said. “We are communicating directly with staff affected by these latest changes and will have more to say in the days ahead.”
This story has been updated with additional details.

articles.title: Houthis launch attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Aden - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Houthis launch attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Aden  Al JazeeraSee more headlines & perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
Houthi fighters have launched a series of attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia and the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in Aden.
In a Facebook post on Saturday, the Yemeni government’s Transport Ministry denounced what it described as the Houthis’ targeting of Aden International Airport with two ballistic missiles, calling it the “fourth such attack this month”.
The airport attacks pose “a threat to the safety of civil aviation” and have “humanitarian and economic repercussions for citizens” who rely on it, the ministry warned.
Yemeni authorities said that the coastguard headquarters and a second building were also hit.
The Houthis claimed attacks on the al-Nasr camp and Aden’s naval military base.
Yemen’s army said a Houthi missile killed three people when it malfunctioned and fell on a family home in Houthi-held Sanaa on Friday. The army said it was one of a number of missile malfunctions seen in recent weeks by the Iran-backed group.
Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV said on Saturday that Saudi coalition air strikes killed several civilians in Sanaa and in the port city of Hodeidah. The claim could not be verified and Riyadh has not commented on the alleged raids.
Saudi attacks
Also on Saturday, Saudi Arabia’s civil defence said on X that the Houthis had launched two ballistic missiles towards Mecca and Medina, warning of “the fall of shrapnel” following their interception.
Images shared on X by the Saudi Press Agency appeared to show a large, blackened missile-shaped object that had landed somewhere in Saudi Arabia.
Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, Secretary-General of the Gulf Cooperation Council, described the Houthi attacks as “heinous”, which embody “a blatant disregard for the lives and security of civilians” in a statement shared on Saturday.
The Houthis said the claim that they targeted the two cities – the holiest in Islam – was a “huge lie”. They said their targets were three Saudi airports, oil infrastructure, and an airbase.
The Houthis have persistently targeted Saudi energy infrastructure and airports across the country with long-range strikes since a fragile ceasefire agreed in 2022 fell apart in July.
Fighting rages
Intense fighting is continuing on Yemen’s front lines as the Houthis battle forces of the internationally recognised government for control of key areas.
On Saturday, Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said that government forces had carried out more than 700 “targeting operations” over the last 24 hours across Yemen, “neutralising” 300 Houthi fighters and disabling military vehicles.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify those figures.
Operations targeted field command centres, Houthi gatherings, weapons depots, and supply lines in Taiz, where intense clashes have been ongoing for days, the spokesman added.

articles.title: Why the USA is refusing to support Saudi Arabia against the Houthis - North East Bylines
articles.summary: Why the USA is refusing to support Saudi Arabia against the Houthis  North East Bylines
articles.full_text:
In the last week, the Houthi rebels in Yemen have successfully launched multiple strikes on Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid Airport in its capital city, Riyadh. Since 2023, the Houthis have increased their activity in response to the Israeli government’s campaign in Gaza. The conflict has had impacts far beyond the region due to the strategic importance of its geography to the World economy. The Houthi rebels control much of Northern and Western Yemen, which looks out into the Red Sea; through which nearly 15% of all global shipping passes. Following the hijacking of a commercial ship by Houthi rebels in 2023, as well as dozens of drone and missile attacks on other vessels, major shipping companies have now rerouted to longer, more costly routes, hindering efforts to drive down the cost-of-living-crisis affecting much of the world.
It seems strange then, given his determination to have shipping lanes in the Middle East re-opened, and to bring down Iran’s proxies, that when the Saudi Arabian Government requested help from the USA to drive back the Houthis, Donald Trump refused.
Who are the Houthis, and why are they fighting Saudi Arabia?
The Houthis are an armed political group in Yemen who are backed by Iran, and position themselves against the West. The group represents the country’s Shia minority, the Zaidis. In 2014, they rebelled against the Yemeni government and occupied the nation’s capital Sanaa. Fearing an Iranian-backed militia taking control of Yemen, Saudi Arabia formed a coalition of Arab states that intervened in support of Yemen’s government. The resulting war created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, but failed to break the Houthis. A ceasefire mediated by the UN took effect in 2022, but following Israel’s response to the October 7th attacks, the Houthis began firing missiles and drones towards Israel and merchant ships in the Red Sea. The US, UK and Israel commenced air strikes on the group in response until the US and Houthis reached a deal to stop targeting one another in 2025.
Earlier this year, the Houthis announced a maritime embargo against the Saudis and began missile and drone attacks against the country in response to what they see as a years-long Saudi blockade. Most recently, the Houthis have launched successful strikes against the airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital city Riyadh, and have taken control of an important shipping channel – the Bab al-Mandab Strait. It is reported that the Saudis have sought help from the USA against the Houthis and while Trump has condemned the Houthi advance, he has so far rejected any military response.
Why is America refusing to help?
On the surface, the decision of the United States not to help out a gulf ally seems confusing. The Houthis are threatening a global shipping lane which has become ever more important following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and their attacks give the US a legitimate reason to launch strikes on another of Iran’s proxy groups and, if successful, weaken their influence in the region. However, when one considers the position that Donald Trump finds himself in domestically, the picture becomes a lot clearer.
The midterm elections are approaching in the US, and they come at a bad time for the President. Since the beginning of the War with Iran, prices of fuel and gasoline have more than doubled. The impacts have been felt by the American people and they blame Trump and his war. Disapproval ratings of Trump have reached 70% on the economy and 64% disapprove of his foreign policy. The Republicans are clearly aware of the impact the war in the Middle East is having on their electability, and already Trump has declared that there will be no more strikes on Iran until after the election. Military action against the Houthis would not only bring attention back to the Middle East, but would also risk opening up a new front in the war against Iran, which the White House desperately wants to end.
The Houthis have also played their part in keeping the US out of its war with Saudi Arabia by promising the safety of US vessels in the Red Sea, claiming only Saudi ships will be targeted by their blockade. This promise goes back to the ceasefire deal struck between the rebels and the US in 2025. Trump clearly does not see antagonising the rebels by breaking the deal as a risk worth taking, in regard to both the upcoming elections and the reopening of Middle East shipping channels.
What’s next?
The Saudi leadership now faces a difficult choice between continued military operations, which it can scarcely afford, or diplomatic resolution, which could leave it with a stronger Houthi government on its southern border. The missile strikes have also impacted the Kingdom’s attempts to diversify their economy, given the global move away from oil as Riyadh has been forced to postpone its ‘Davos in the Desert’ conference scheduled for the end of this month in the wake of the Houthi attacks. By refusing to provide support to Riyadh, the US is leaving an ally hanging out to dry in the face of deadly missile attacks, while at the same time, making deals with their enemies.

articles.title: Oil prices jump $3 on Houthi attacks, oil spill, highest settlement since April - The Morning
articles.summary: Oil prices jump $3 on Houthi attacks, oil spill, highest settlement since April  The Morning
articles.full_text:
Oil prices settled more than $3 higher on Friday, their highest in nearly six months after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East, where UAE authorities also reported an oil spill.
Brent crude futures settled at $116.72 a barrel, up $3.55 or 3.14%, their highest since April 29. US West Texas Intermediate crude closed at $103.27 a barrel, up $3.80 or 3.8%.
Brent finished the week up 6% and WTI ended 2.3% higher.
"Fears of supply disruptions drove the advance after Iranian-backed Houthi rebels carried out a series of attacks across Saudi Arabia, including on energy infrastructure," said Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for LPL Financial.
On Thursday, Saudi Aramco ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported. Fighting intensified between Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen-based Houthis.
An oil spill from a tanker was detected off the UAE coast of Umm Al Quwain, the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said.
It did not say what caused the spill and authorities have not identified the tanker involved.
ATTACKS ON VESSELS
Shipping sources said on October 9 that the Gem No. 2 supertanker was struck by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles (24 km) west of Al Jazeera in the UAE.
"The market is concerned about these continued Iranian attacks on tankers that we've seen increase over the last week," said Andrew Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. “While there has been an increase in oil transiting out of the Strait of Hormuz, that could change at any minute.”
Clashes between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government have raged since the Iran-aligned Houthis pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb Strait last month, a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea.
October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017.
President Donald Trump said on Friday the US could end the war with Iran quickly, but said perhaps Washington should allow the conflict to gradually wind down.
STRATEGIC RESERVE RELEASES
The US Department of Energy said it had authorized an emergency exchange of up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address a supply disruption affecting Phillips 66's Lake Charles refinery in Louisiana.
The SPR is already at the lowest level since 1982 after President Donald Trump tapped it as the US war on Iran disrupted supply lines. Trump's predecessor, President Joe Biden, also tapped the SPR following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Elsewhere, Germany's national oil stockpiling agency EBV circulated a tender to sell diesel, heating oil and crude oil volumes from strategic reserves.
This marks Germany's first oil releases from strategic reserves since G7 countries, under pressure from Trump, agreed to do so at the start of October.
On Thursday, the head of Libya's National Oil Corp told Reuters that an oil pipeline valve from the Hamada and Tahara oilfields to Zawiya port had been shut, leading to a reduction in production at both fields.
Ship tracking data showed the first Russian diesel bound for the US since Moscow and Washington reached an export agreement was aboard a tanker heading for New York.
Trump announced the deal this month as part of efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of US midterm elections on November 3.
US energy firms this week kept the total rig count unchanged for a second week in a row, energy services firm Baker Hughes said in its closely followed report on Friday. The total oil and gas rig count, an early indicator of future output, held steady at 603 during the week ended October 23.
Source: Reuters

articles.title: Merz warns of threat from Russia amid Germany's political turmoil
articles.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned Saturday that Russia was seeking to destabilize Germany through cyberattacks, sabotage and other threats, urging his struggling coalition to...
articles.full_text:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned Saturday that Russia was seeking to destabilize Germany through cyberattacks, sabotage and other threats, urging his struggling coalition to unite behind economic reforms and defend the country's security.
Speaking at a convention of the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of his Christian Democratic Union (CDU), in Munich, Merz described the security situation in Europe as increasingly dangerous and called for a stronger response to threats from abroad and political extremism at home.
"We are facing a massive threat in the east of our continent. Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine has profoundly shaken the European peace order," Merz said.
"And we also see that Russia seeks to destabilize Germany, day in and day out," he added.
Merz said the threat extended beyond the war in Ukraine, pointing to cyberattacks, sabotage and attempted attacks against critical infrastructure across Europe. He cited an attempted drone attack involving a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig Airport on Aug. 4 as an example of the risks facing Germany.
"This threat is no longer limited to Ukraine," Merz said, warning that such operations also sought to undermine democratic institutions and weaken public confidence.
"All of this threatens our freedom, and that is why we are investing in preserving our freedom," he added.
Russia has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is conducting a campaign of hybrid warfare against Germany and other European countries. Relations between Berlin and Moscow have deteriorated sharply since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Merz's warning followed remarks by Germany's foreign intelligence chief, Martin Jaeger, who told parliament's intelligence committee on Oct. 5 that the confrontation with Russia had entered a more dangerous phase.
"Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia. The attempted attack in Leipzig is only one example of that," Jaeger said.
"No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany," he added.
Merz's security warning came as his government faced mounting political pressure following poor regional election results and declining public approval.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) finished first in two eastern German states, while the far-left Left Party topped the vote in Berlin, highlighting the growing challenge facing the country's mainstream political parties.
Merz's approval ratings have fallen to record lows, while disagreements have intensified within the governing coalition and between the CDU and CSU. Although the two conservative parties have a long history of internal disputes, they have generally managed to maintain their alliance.
At the Munich convention, Merz praised CSU ministers serving in his government and paid tribute to CSU leader Markus Soeder in an effort to reinforce ties between the conservative partners.
He also reiterated his opposition to cooperating with the AfD, which leads national opinion polls. Some conservatives have called for a reassessment of the party's political isolation, but Merz insisted that working with the far right was incompatible with membership in the conservative alliance.
"Any politician who votes with the AfD has no place in our Union," he said.
Merz also urged the Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens not to form a coalition with the Left Party in Berlin, accusing the party of tolerating antisemitism within its ranks. The Left Party denies that antisemitism is systemic within the organization.
The conference also exposed lingering disagreements over the succession to German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, whose term is due to end next year.
Delegates applauded when Merz mentioned Ilse Aigner, a CSU politician proposed by the Bavarian party as its candidate for the largely ceremonial presidency. The CDU has not endorsed Aigner, and party sources say it has not ruled out putting forward its own candidate.
Beyond security concerns, Merz urged his coalition partners to move quickly on reforms to Germany's pension, tax and welfare systems, arguing that economic recovery was essential to restoring confidence in public institutions.
He said the conservative parties had a responsibility to strengthen Germany's social stability by addressing structural economic problems and implementing reforms that could revive growth.
The government has faced growing criticism over its economic performance, adding to the political challenges confronting Merz as his coalition struggles to maintain public support.
His appeal for unity reflected the pressure on the chancellor to demonstrate that his government can respond to security threats while tackling domestic economic concerns and preventing further gains by extremist parties.

articles.title: 7 trapped after 16-storey building collapses in Kenya's Nairobi
articles.summary: Rescue teams were searching for seven people feared trapped after a 16-storey building under construction collapsed Friday in Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, Interior Minister Kipchumba...
articles.full_text:
Rescue teams were searching for seven people feared trapped after a 16-storey building under construction collapsed Friday in Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen said.
Videos circulating online showed the building suddenly crumbling, sending massive clouds of dust into the air in Eastleigh, a densely populated area with a mix of residential and commercial buildings.
The structure was reduced to a heap of rubble as emergency crews rushed to the scene. Rescuers faced difficulties accessing the site, which was wedged between other high-rise buildings.
“Eleven shops on the ground floor and in the basement were occupied at the time of the collapse. Seven people have been reported missing,” Murkomen wrote in a post on X late Friday.
He said 66 of the 67 people working at the construction site had escaped unharmed, while one person was injured.
Earlier, police said they had rescued a woman from the rubble and could hear another person calling for help.
“The contractors and the engineers are supposed to ensure that the works are followed by professionals. But most are not,” Bibiye Mahmoud, president of the Institution of Engineering Technology of Kenya, told Agence France-Presse (AFP) at the scene.
“This is why we are seeing these catastrophes ... There is no accountability,” she added.
A report by Kenya’s National Building Inspectorate found that 87% of buildings audited nationwide last year failed to meet standards or lacked the required approvals.
“Our concern is to save lives,” Nairobi Gov. Johnson Sakaja told reporters, adding, “This building has no occupation certificate ... this has potentially cost lives.”
An occupation certificate is formal approval from the relevant authorities confirming that a building is safe and legally fit for occupancy.
John Ogallo, vice president of the Institution of Engineers of Kenya, who was also at the scene, said there had been warning signs before the collapse.
“People here are saying distresses were observed, like cracks,” he told reporters.
If a building is constructed with the wrong materials, “it becomes a time bomb,” he added.
Nairobi is experiencing a construction boom, with high-rise buildings springing up across the city, particularly in Eastleigh, known for its busy markets and large Somali community.
The number of buildings completed annually in Nairobi rose from 20,025 in 2022 to 25,090 last year, according to the country’s statistics bureau, as East Africa’s leading business hub attracts people from rural areas and neighboring countries.
Local media reported looting shortly after the collapse, which occurred around lunchtime.
AFP journalists saw police use tear gas to disperse crowds gathering near the site.
A report by the Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis documented 86 building collapses in Nairobi between 2009 and 2019, resulting in an estimated 200 deaths.
Corruption has allowed contractors to cut corners and bypass building regulations.
Five people were killed when a six-storey building collapsed in a town on the outskirts of Nairobi in September 2022.
In April 2016, 49 people died when a six-storey apartment building collapsed in the northeastern part of the capital after days of heavy rain caused flooding and landslides.

articles.title: Harris returns to campaign trail as 2028 White House questions loom
articles.summary: Kamala Harris is stepping back into the political arena to help Democrats compete in closely contested midterm races as the former vice president weighs whether to seek the preside...
articles.full_text:
Kamala Harris is stepping back into the political arena to help Democrats compete in closely contested midterm races as the former vice president weighs whether to seek the presidency again in 2028.
Harris, the Democrats’ unsuccessful 2024 presidential nominee, has made relatively few public appearances this year.
But with the party seeking to break Republicans’ hold on Congress ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, she is campaigning in Georgia, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and Wisconsin. The tour could renew speculation about her political ambitions as a growing field of potential 2028 presidential contenders begins to emerge.
She launched the tour Tuesday in Las Vegas with a new stump speech criticizing what she described as President Donald Trump’s cruelty, while drawing on the aspirational messaging that has long defined her public appearances. Harris made history as the first woman and the first Black and South Asian American to serve as vice president.
She spoke to scores of Culinary Workers Union members alongside gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford, Nevada’s first Black attorney general. Harris said Ford would become the “first Black governor west of the Mississippi” if elected.
“We got a serious fight in front of us,” Harris said. “We are witnessing pure brutality come out of what is undoubtedly the most corrupt, callous and incompetent presidential administration.”
Like Trump, who is traveling around the country to campaign for Republican candidates, Harris is not broadly popular among voters. A Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll in June showed that 39% of Americans viewed her favorably, but the figures were sharply divided along partisan lines: 82% of Democrats viewed her favorably, compared with 7% of Republicans and 33% of independents.
“At the end of a campaign, you bring out your heavy hitters,” said Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and a member of the Democratic National Committee. “That’s what’s going on here with her, and frankly with Trump.”
The day after her Las Vegas appearance, Harris led chants of “Mississippi matters!” before a crowd supporting Scott Colom in Columbus, Mississippi. Colom is seeking to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since 1982. Polls show an unusually tight race with Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Harris opened with advice she said she gives young people she mentors: “Never let someone else’s limited ability to see your capacity be a limitation on your ambition,” she said. “Let me repeat that.” She repeated the line more loudly, drawing cheers from the crowd.
If Harris decides to run for the White House again in 2028, she would likely be among the most high-profile names in what is expected to be a crowded Democratic field.
But Harris also carries the baggage of past defeats. She lost the 2024 presidential election to Trump, and her first presidential campaign ended before the 2020 Democratic nominating contests began.
A 2028 campaign would also force Harris to revisit the Democrats’ tumultuous 2024 race, when then-President Joe Biden abruptly ended his reelection campaign amid questions about his health and mental acuity, and Harris replaced him as the party’s nominee.
Harris has since called Biden’s decision to seek reelection “reckless” in her memoir, “107 Days,” a reference to the short campaign she inherited. This month, she offered her clearest criticism yet of Biden’s support for Israel’s war in Gaza, rebuking the Israeli government’s “horrific conduct” and saying the U.S. should have “acted sooner and more forcefully.”
“All these things will be relitigated,” Kamarck said. “What happened to Biden? Did she know? Did she think he was losing it? And on and on and on.”
Scott Ferson, a Democratic strategist and author of “How the Democrats Lost America,” said the party has tended to give short shrift to candidates who have lost elections. However, voters disillusioned with Trump may also view Harris in a new light.
“She has that kind of crossover appeal,” Ferson said, “particularly with people who left in 2024 or stayed home.” Her implicit message, he suggested, is: “Do you regret staying home?”
Earlier this month, as Harris wrapped up an appearance on the “Baby, This Is Keke Palmer” video podcast, Palmer asked whether she would run again.
“Oh, girl, come on!” Harris said, laughing as she gripped the hands of the Hollywood star. “I haven’t decided yet.”
“But the midterms, the midterms, the midterms,” Harris continued. “2028 don’t matter if we don’t do 2026 right.”

articles.title: More than 2,000 flee Ethiopia clashes as death toll reaches 9
articles.summary: Ethnic clashes in southern Ethiopia have forced more than 2,000 people to flee across the border into neighboring Kenya, with at least nine deaths reported as violence continued, o...
articles.full_text:
Ethnic clashes in southern Ethiopia have forced more than 2,000 people to flee across the border into neighboring Kenya, with at least nine deaths reported as violence continued, officials said Friday.
Stanley Kamande, commissioner of Kenya’s Marsabit County, said thousands of Ethiopians had crossed into the border town of Moyale after armed clashes broke out on the Ethiopian side of the frontier on Wednesday.
Reports from Ethiopia said at least nine people had been killed and dozens wounded in the fighting. The casualty figures could not be independently verified.
The violence involves ethnic Oromo and Somali communities following tensions over the display of the Somali Regional State flag in an area administered by Ethiopia’s Oromia region.
Both are federal regions of Ethiopia, distinct from the neighboring country of Somalia, which shares borders with Ethiopia and Kenya.
A woman in Moyale was also reportedly injured by a bullet fired from across the border and received medical treatment.
The Kenya Red Cross said Thursday it was providing emergency assistance to displaced families, initially targeting 1,000 households.
The organization said it was working with government authorities to provide temporary shelter, food, clean water and other essential supplies.
Moyale, a major border crossing between the two East African countries, lies 780 kilometers (485 miles) north of Nairobi, Kenya’s capital, and 775 kilometers (482 miles) south of Addis Ababa, Ethiopia’s capital.
The unrest has raised concerns about further displacement and disruption to cross-border trade.

articles.title: Kenya Ebola outbreak claims 2nd life as 9 cases confirmed
articles.summary: Kenya confirmed its second Ebola death Friday after a 65-year-old woman died while receiving treatment at an infectious disease facility, the Health Ministry said, bringing the dea...
articles.full_text:
Kenya confirmed its second Ebola death Friday after a 65-year-old woman died while receiving treatment at an infectious disease facility, the Health Ministry said, bringing the death toll to two among nine confirmed cases.
The woman, Kenya’s third confirmed Ebola case, died late Friday, according to a statement by Director General for Health Patrick Amoth.
“The Ministry of Health is deeply saddened to announce the passing on of a 65-year-old female patient, the third confirmed case of Ebola (Bundibugyo virus disease) in Kenya,” Amoth said.
The woman was a close family member and direct contact of Kenya’s first Ebola patient, who also died from the disease.
She had been placed in quarantine before developing symptoms on Oct. 13 and was admitted to an infectious disease treatment unit that same day.
Health officials said she had been receiving supportive care but died after her condition deteriorated.
The ministry said it was arranging a safe burial in consultation with the family. Specialized teams were expected to conduct the burial under established infection-prevention protocols.
The latest death leaves seven Ebola patients receiving care at two isolation facilities, according to the ministry.
Authorities said all nine infections were linked to a single group of known contacts, with no indication that the virus had spread to the wider population.
“All cases remain within one cluster of known contacts, and there is no evidence of community spread,” the ministry said.
Kenya confirmed its first Ebola infection earlier this month, prompting increased disease surveillance, contact tracing and quarantine measures to prevent further transmission.
Authorities continue to monitor people who may have been exposed to the virus.

articles.title: Jordan vows crackdown after church funeral attack kills 8
articles.summary: Jordan’s King Abdullah vowed a forceful response after gunmen killed eight people and wounded 40 others during a funeral service at a Greek Orthodox church in the southern Karak go...
articles.full_text:
Jordan’s King Abdullah vowed a forceful response after gunmen killed eight people and wounded 40 others during a funeral service at a Greek Orthodox church in the southern Karak governorate, prompting a security crackdown as authorities hunted for the attackers.
The assailants opened fire for several minutes in broad daylight Friday, targeting mourners at the church in an attack that officials described as an act of extremist terrorism. No group immediately claimed responsibility.
King Abdullah visited Karak hours after the attack and ordered security forces to pursue those responsible, promising they would face an “iron fist,” according to the royal court. He also condemned what he called a “despicable terrorist act,” stressing that there could be no leniency when Jordanian lives were at stake.
The king chaired a National Security Council meeting to discuss the attack and the security response.
Authorities said it was too early to determine whether the gunmen had links to known militant groups inside or outside Jordan. Security forces continued searching for the suspects Saturday, while police increased patrols around the church, located about 120 kilometers (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman.
Security was also tightened at shopping malls, foreign embassies and other locations across the kingdom, the U.S. Embassy in Amman said.
At a hospital treating the wounded, Tarek Ammarin described the attack as a massacre. A relative of his was among those injured.
“A massacre, a massacre in every sense of the word,” he said.
Prime Minister Jafar Hassan condemned the violence, blaming what he described as a terrorist ideology and religious extremism.
“We will not allow society to go down this path,” Hassan said in a post on X.
Bahjat al-Rushda, mayor of Shihan village in Karak, also denounced the attack and expressed confidence in the country’s security.
“God willing, this country will remain secure,” he said.
The shooting was a rare attack in Jordan, a key U.S. partner in the fight against terrorist groups. Authorities have said they thwarted several terrorist plots in recent years, although investigators had not established whether the latest attack was connected to any known organization.
Christians make up a minority of Jordan’s population, and the kingdom is home to several biblical sites that draw pilgrims from around the world. The attack raised concerns about the safety of the country’s Christian community and the potential for extremist violence to undermine its longstanding religious coexistence.
Jordan has also faced heightened regional security pressures this year. The kingdom has been among U.S. allies in the Middle East targeted by Iranian attacks following U.S. and Israeli strikes against Iran in February.
Investigators continued their search for the gunmen as officials pledged to hold those responsible accountable.

articles.title: Students join Albania’s ‘Flamingo Revolution’ as unrest spreads
articles.summary: Anti-government protesters gathered in Albania’s capital on Saturday as months of demonstrations over corruption, economic hardship and environmental concerns escalated into violen...
articles.full_text:
Anti-government protesters gathered in Albania’s capital on Saturday as months of demonstrations over corruption, economic hardship and environmental concerns escalated into violent clashes, posing the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government in more than a decade.
The latest demonstrations in Tirana followed a week of confrontations involving students, riot police and protesters who set fires, damaged public buildings and clashed with security forces.
What began in May as a campaign against a controversial coastal tourism development has grown into a broader movement demanding political accountability and better living conditions.
The protests, known as the “Flamingo Revolution,” initially focused on a luxury tourism project linked to Affinity Partners, an investment firm associated with Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump. The proposed development on Albania’s southern Adriatic coast has drawn environmental objections over its potential impact on protected wetlands and habitats supporting flamingos and other wildlife.
Demonstrators argued that the project threatened ecologically sensitive areas around Sazan Island and the Vjosa-Narta region. Peaceful gatherings in central Tirana continued for more than 130 days, with protesters using flamingo imagery as a symbol of their opposition.
Over time, the movement expanded beyond environmental concerns, incorporating allegations of corruption, dissatisfaction with public services, economic grievances and calls for Rama to resign.
The unrest intensified in mid-October when high school and university students joined the demonstrations in large numbers. They cited rising education costs, inadequate university facilities and dormitories, limited financial assistance and poor employment prospects after graduation, alongside the broader cost-of-living crisis.
Marches initially focused on the Education Ministry but soon turned violent. Protesters smashed windows, burned trash bins and kiosks, and damaged bank branches and government buildings. Among the targeted sites was a Raiffeisen bank branch.
Some demonstrators threw rocks, fireworks and flares at police, while others used Molotov cocktails. Riot police responded with tear gas, water cannons and baton charges. By around Oct. 17, security forces also appeared to be using rubber bullets, according to reports from the demonstrations.
The confrontations continued for several days, spreading beyond the capital to cities including Durrës, Shkodër, Lezhë, Vlora, Elbasan, Korçë and Gjirokastër.
In Tirana, protesters targeted the Education Ministry, Interior Ministry, Supreme Court and headquarters of the governing Socialist Party. Clashes also erupted near a police station and areas surrounding the prime minister’s office.
Smoke, broken glass, debris and burned barricades littered parts of the capital as security forces struggled to contain the unrest.
Official figures reported during the peak of the clashes indicated hundreds of injuries, including a substantial number of police officers. One tally put the number of injured at about 295, including approximately 186 officers, although subsequent reports cited additional casualties.
Authorities also carried out mass arrests, with reports at the height of the unrest indicating more than 1,000 detentions and nearly 400 criminal prosecutions. Many detainees were subsequently released. Some police officers were suspended amid allegations of excessive force.
Rama, whose Socialist Party has governed Albania since 2013, has rejected demands to step down. He won a fourth term in the 2025 parliamentary elections and has argued that governments must change through democratic elections rather than street violence.
He has portrayed the unrest as a threat to Albania’s democratic stability and its ambition to join the European Union, with membership targeted for the end of the decade.
Rama has also accused unidentified “dark forces,” foreign actors and elements associated with the opposition of exploiting or radicalizing the demonstrations. He has raised concerns about disinformation and possible foreign interference, including alleged involvement by Russia, Iran or other actors. Independent evidence supporting those allegations remains limited.
While condemning arson and attacks on public property, Rama has offered dialogue on students’ concerns, including education costs. He has also defended the police response and announced support for officers, including bonuses and prospective pay increases.
The unrest has disrupted parliamentary proceedings, with sessions canceled or affected by the security situation around government institutions.
Despite the growing violence, many protesters have expressed distrust of the entire political establishment, not only Rama’s government. Demonstrators, many of them young and organizing through loosely coordinated networks rather than a single leadership structure, have rejected both the ruling Socialists and the opposition Democratic Party led by Sali Berisha.
Chants demanding Rama’s resignation have accompanied calls for broader political change, with some protesters invoking revolution and rejecting the country’s two dominant political camps.
The movement’s decentralized character has made it difficult for political leaders to claim control over the demonstrations or present themselves as representatives of the protesters’ demands.
University professors and civil society figures have also criticized aspects of the police response. Some have called for a caretaker government, reflecting concerns that the crisis extends beyond individual policy disputes to wider questions about political accountability and institutional trust.
Albania’s longstanding problems with corruption, employment opportunities and living standards have helped fuel public dissatisfaction. The latest unrest has brought those concerns together with anger over education and environmental protection, turning a campaign against one development project into a wider confrontation over the country’s political direction.
Saturday’s planned gatherings included an opposition rally in central Tirana around midday, student demonstrations and solidarity actions near the Education Ministry, and activities involving university lecturers, including those associated with the Polytechnic University.
The events followed days of tension after the initial wave of violent confrontations. Authorities also reportedly increased border checks in some areas as the situation remained unsettled.
The protests present a significant test for Rama as Albania pursues EU membership and seeks to maintain political stability. Although the government has insisted that the unrest will not determine its future, the scale of the demonstrations and the breadth of the grievances have underscored the depth of public discontent.

articles.title: French police fire tear gas, security personnel deploy for protests
articles.summary: French police fired tear gas at protesters Saturday as authorities deployed 70,000 security personnel across the country to prevent a repeat of last weekend’s riots and looting, am...
articles.full_text:
French police fired tear gas at protesters Saturday as authorities deployed 70,000 security personnel across the country to prevent a repeat of last weekend’s riots and looting, amid renewed demonstrations over the rising cost of living and growing political tensions ahead of next year’s presidential election.
In the southeastern city of Lyon, police used tear gas to disperse about 150 protesters near the city center after some briefly attempted to block a road in an area where demonstrations had been banned, an Agence France-Presse (AFP) journalist witnessed.
Authorities across France tightened security as businesses prepared for possible violence, with memories of last weekend’s clashes still fresh. Police equipped with riot gear were deployed in areas previously affected by vandalism and looting, while retailers took precautions to protect their properties.
The Interior Ministry said 70,000 security personnel had been mobilized nationwide in response to what it described as a high risk of violence.
“We will not tolerate any unrest,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said Friday, warning that social media posts had circulated calls for violence and looting.
In Paris, many shops boarded up their windows, and some major retailers notified customers they would remain closed Saturday. Near the Bastille neighborhood, a clothing store removed all its merchandise from display shelves, while a nearby restaurant covered its windows with boards but put up signs assuring customers it remained open.
The Louvre and Musee d’Orsay museums were also closed as security concerns disrupted activity in the capital.
Paris police ordered a union-organized march to be moved at the last minute from the central-eastern Bastille area to Porte d’Italie, on the southeastern edge of the city. Unions said they would reluctantly accept the relocation, while the Yellow Vest movement, which led disruptive protests against President Emmanuel Macron in 2018, indicated it would defy the order.
Protests target Macron and the far right
Saturday’s demonstrations also took aim at Macron and Marine Le Pen, whose far-right National Rally party was holding a congress in the central city of Orleans to launch its campaign for presidential elections scheduled in six months.
Thousands of demonstrators marched against Le Pen and Macron, chanting slogans including “Macron resign. Le Pen in prison.”
The olitical tensions reflect an increasingly volatile atmosphere ahead of the vote, with opinion polls suggesting Le Pen is well positioned to succeed Macron, who cannot seek a third consecutive term.
Organizers of the nationwide demonstrations accuse Macron’s government of failing to address public anger over rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. Inflation has intensified pressure on households across France, with the war in the Middle East, launched in February by U.S. President Donald Trump and Israel, contributing to the surge in prices.
Last weekend’s demonstrations descended into violence in several locations as groups on the fringes of the protests clashed with police, vandalized public buildings and looted hundreds of shops. Authorities arrested about 2,700 people, while retailers estimated that damage and stolen merchandise had cost the sector hundreds of millions of euros.
Macron blamed the worst violence on what he described as “ultra-left” groups seeking to undermine the French Republic.
His government has sought to distinguish peaceful demonstrations and legitimate grievances from the vandalism, arson and looting that accompanied last weekend’s unrest. Macron has said authorities would accept union-led demonstrations while cracking down on gatherings they consider illegitimate.
French courts have already sentenced 217 people to prison over the previous weekend’s violence, officials said. About half were first-time offenders.
Authorities in Marseille initially banned all protests but announced Friday that a union-organized demonstration would be permitted as an exception.
Rights groups question protest restrictions
The tightening of restrictions has drawn criticism from human rights organizations, which warn that broad bans and police measures could undermine the right to peaceful assembly.
Amnesty International condemned what it called “a slide toward authoritarian practice,” arguing that the measures jeopardized the right to demonstrate peacefully.
Eva Cosse, a senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch, said authorities had a responsibility to balance public safety with the protection of demonstrators’ rights.
“Police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder,” Cosse said.
The unrest comes amid a wider wave of demonstrations across Europe, including in Italy, Belgium, Spain and Portugal, where protesters have raised concerns over different issues, with inflation and education among the recurring grievances. Italy has deployed 500 troops to help contain street violence in Milan.

articles.title: Paris closes museums as France deploys police for fresh protests
articles.summary: Major museums in Paris closed Saturday as authorities deployed tens of thousands of police officers across France ahead of a new round of protests, seeking to prevent a repeat of l...
articles.full_text:
Major museums in Paris closed Saturday as authorities deployed tens of thousands of police officers across France ahead of a new round of protests, seeking to prevent a repeat of last week’s violent unrest that shocked the country.
Last week’s demonstrations were marked by looting, torched cars and attacks on public buildings, with masked groups targeting businesses in Paris and other major cities, raising questions about the government’s ability to maintain order.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said up to 70,000 officers would be deployed nationwide, backed by helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.
Authorities braced for another large turnout after more than 500,000 people took to the streets across France last week.
Major museums, including the Louvre, the Orsay Museum, the Picasso Museum and the Grand Palais, where a major Cezanne exhibition is on display, were closed Saturday. Art Basel, one of the world’s leading contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday but canceled its weekend program amid concerns about unrest.
Parisian shopkeepers had been barricading their stores throughout the week. Near Place de la R
epublique, one of last weekend’s protest hot spots, a bank branch and other businesses were boarded up with wooden panels to deter potential looters.
Following the unrest, Paris police prefect Patrice Faure urged shopkeepers to hire security guards. He later clarified that protecting business owners and their establishments was the government’s responsibility.
About 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted last weekend.
Protest marches were scheduled in Paris and Marseille, while local authorities banned some other rallies, including those planned in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier. Cities outside Paris were also hit hard by the unrest. In Limoges, a suspected arson attack nearly destroyed the 19th-century city hall.
Trade unions criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the French Constitution.
President Emmanuel Macron, a centrist, entered the crisis in the final stretch of his term, with his popularity at its lowest level since he took office in 2017. He has said the measures are necessary to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.
Saturday’s demonstration in Orleans, about 110 kilometers (70 miles) south of Paris, was also expected to draw close attention.
About 50 organizations called for a protest against the far right on the sidelines of a two-day congress of Marine Le Pen’s nationalist, anti-immigration party, ahead of next spring’s presidential election. The organizers included labor unions, left-wing parties, student groups and anti-racism organizations.
The demonstrations began last month at a high school southeast of Paris over staff shortages.
Class boycotts and demonstrations subsequently spread to other Paris suburbs and across the country, including smaller towns. High school students raised concerns about underfunded schools and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighborhoods. Some also called for reforms to the university admissions system, which many consider unfair.
As the government struggled to respond to students’ demands, the movement expanded into broader protests over the rising cost of living, just months before voters are due to choose Macron’s successor.
“The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people,” said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University. “And it’s not possible anymore.”

articles.title: Kim’s surprise China trip raises hopes of renewed US talks
articles.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un returned home Saturday after an unannounced visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong, where he attended a ceremony honoring Chinese soldiers kill...
articles.full_text:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un returned home Saturday after an unannounced visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong, where he attended a ceremony honoring Chinese soldiers killed in the Korean War and visited an automobile factory, according to Chinese state media.
The purpose of the daylong trip remained unclear, with neither Pyongyang nor Beijing announcing the visit in advance. There was no official confirmation that Kim met Chinese President Xi Jinping or Premier Li Qiang.
China’s Xinhua News Agency reported that Wang Huning, the country’s top political adviser, accompanied Kim during his visit and saw him off at the border bridge as he departed. Wang Yi, China’s top diplomat, also participated in the events.
South Korean lawmaker Youn Kun-young said he had received a briefing on Friday indicating that Kim was likely to visit China. Citing information he had received, Youn said Kim was understood to have met Li on Saturday, although Chinese state media did not confirm such a meeting.
Youn said the visit could send a “positive signal” about the possibility of a summit between Kim and U.S. President Donald Trump.
Speculation has grown that the two leaders could meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit scheduled for November in Shenzhen, China. Such a meeting could revive diplomatic efforts over North Korea’s nuclear program, although no summit has been confirmed.
China remains North Korea’s largest trading partner and a crucial source of economic, political and diplomatic support for the isolated country, which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear weapons program.
Xinhua quoted Wang as saying Kim’s visit was important for consolidating public goodwill toward the longstanding friendship between the two countries, strengthening political trust and expanding cooperation.
Wang also called for closer exchanges between their populations, deeper economic cooperation and stronger strategic coordination to protect their respective sovereignty, security and development interests. He conveyed Xi’s greetings and best wishes to Kim.
The trip coincided with the anniversary of China’s entry into the Korean War, when Chinese forces fought alongside North Korea against South Korea and U.S.-led United Nations forces between 1950 and 1953. The conflict ended with an armistice in 1953, leaving the two Koreas technically at war because no peace treaty was signed.
Kim is believed to have entered China across the New Yalu River Bridge, a four-lane crossing spanning about 3 kilometers (1.9 miles) between Dandong and the North Korean city of Sinuiju.
Although construction was completed in 2014, the bridge remained unused for years because North Korea had not completed the necessary connecting roads and customs facilities. Its opening in mid-October marked a new step in efforts to strengthen economic links between the neighboring countries.
The opening came just over a month after North Korea and Russia inaugurated their first road bridge, underscoring Pyongyang’s efforts to deepen infrastructure and economic cooperation with its key partners.
Analysts said Kim’s visit could have been intended to push Beijing to accelerate economic commitments made during Xi’s state visit to North Korea in June.
“He may also have sought Beijing’s active support and cooperation ahead of a possible summit with Trump in Shenzhen,” Yang Moo-jin, former president of South Korea’s University of North Korean Studies, told Agence France-Presse.
Xi’s June visit to Pyongyang followed back-to-back meetings in Beijing with Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, highlighting China’s diplomatic engagement with leaders whose governments have increasingly aligned with North Korea.
The official statements issued after Xi’s meeting with Kim did not mention denuclearization, an omission that analysts interpreted as a possible indication that Beijing was placing less emphasis on the long-standing demand for North Korea to abandon its nuclear arsenal.
Kim’s visit to China came as tensions remained high on the Korean Peninsula, where diplomatic efforts to improve relations have made little progress.
Hours before South Korean media first reported the trip, North Korean state media said Kim had called on his military to train to become the strongest in the world.
Addressing a major military meeting in Pyongyang, Kim urged the armed forces to pursue what he described as a “Korean-style military revolution,” reinforcing his government’s emphasis on military readiness.
His remarks came after South Korea’s military proposed talks with North Korea to clarify the countries’ shared border following an explosion in the heavily fortified Demilitarized Zone.
Seoul blamed the blast, which injured South Korean soldiers, on North Korean landmines. Pyongyang has strongly rejected the accusation.
South Korea proposed military talks Friday, but North Korea had not responded to the offer. Pyongyang has also rejected Seoul’s demand for an apology over the incident, further straining relations between the two sides.
The latest tensions complicate efforts by South Korean President Lee Jae Myung to reopen dialogue with the North. Lee has repeatedly offered talks without preconditions as part of a broader effort to ease hostilities.
North Korea’s nuclear arsenal remains a central obstacle to any broader diplomatic settlement involving Pyongyang, Seoul, Washington and Beijing.
Despite years of United Nations sanctions, North Korea has formally established its status as a nuclear-armed state and repeatedly declared that its nuclear weapons program is permanent and irreversible.
In September, Lee suggested that Washington consider seeking a freeze on North Korea’s nuclear program rather than insisting on its immediate elimination, potentially offering sanctions relief in return.
Supporters of such an approach see it as a possible starting point for limiting North Korea’s nuclear capabilities and reducing the risk of conflict. Critics, however, warn that it could amount to tacitly accepting Pyongyang as a nuclear power while allowing it to secure economic concessions without surrendering its weapons.
Analysts say China’s recent diplomatic posture has also raised questions about whether Beijing is moving toward a similar position.
The absence of any reference to denuclearization in the official accounts of Xi’s June visit to Pyongyang reinforced those concerns, although neither government has formally abandoned its stated position on the issue.
Kim’s latest trip to China therefore comes at a sensitive moment, as North Korea seeks to strengthen ties with Beijing, tensions with Seoul remain unresolved and speculation continues over a possible meeting with Trump.
